claims.text: Mechanical-behavior differences between the quinary alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets stem from changes in local lattice distortion and dislocation dynamics.
The quinary alloy has greater atomic-size mismatch than the alloys with fewer constituents.
The greater chemical complexity of the quinary alloy produces higher lattice friction.
Changing from the quinary alloy to quaternary and ternary subsets changes the stacking-fault energy.
The lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy state of the quinary alloy promote planar dislocation slip.
The lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy state of the quinary alloy delay dislocation cross-slip.
Increased atomic misfit in the quinary alloy impedes dislocation motion through enhanced local lattice distortion.
Planar slip, delayed cross-slip, and increased lattice friction give the quinary alloy greater strain hardening than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
All compared alloys are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Similar thermomechanical processing gives the compared alloys comparable grain sizes.
Similar thermomechanical processing gives the compared alloys comparable defect densities.
Composition-dependent short-range chemical ordering mediates dislocation mobility and slip behavior.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strengths than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit more dislocation cross-slip than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will undergo localized deformation earlier than the quinary baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable under single-phase FCC conditions, matched thermomechanical processing, room-temperature testing, and moderate strain rates.
